638826d093.why: Old tell fixed: 'Algae' (killed by 'pure rainwater') is now 'Tiny worms', the old tooth-worm belief, a live and truly wrong lure; the rainwater clause now rules out no choice. The cut closer no longer hints at a new kind. Key true: the letter of 17 September 1683 (white matter 'about as thick as batter', mixed with rain-water and spittle, many small living animalcules moving) 'is often cited as the first unambiguous observation of bacteria' (Lens on Leeuwenhoek). He did not call the tooth creatures worms (he used 'worms' only for nose and face matter), so the lure is not his own word. Viruses are too small for a light lens; mites and worms are many-celled animals. Card's fact-check error fixed: Dutch word for little animals, 'animalcules' the translators' English. Four live choices for a 6th grader; plain 6th-grade cell-theory history; voice clean ('they' in the card is plural).

a27387fc4c.why: Old tell fixed: only one plant-only part (chloroplasts) is left, and 'Its central vacuole' is now 'Its cytoplasm', which every animal cell has but which gives no landmark, so nucleus, cytoplasm and mitochondria stay live for a 6th grader. Closer now asks what he looked for to pick out each cell. Key true: Schleiden held the nucleus the most important part; Schwann reasoned 'the nucleus should also be found in the ultimate particles of animal tissues' and found nuclei 'in abundance' (Williams); Wikipedia: animal tissues 'composed of cells, each of which has a nucleus'; the dinner talk 'turned on the nuclei'. Plant cells easy to see by their thick walls (OpenStax); 1838 and 1839 right. Mitochondria first described 1857 (Kolliker), so wrong for Schwann. Choices parallel; voice clean.

460982845a.why: Overlap fixed: re-keyed on Virchow, the grade's named scientist, not on cells dividing. Honesty holds: Remak's evidence comes first (OpenStax: 1852, 'convincing evidence that cells are derived from other cells as a result of cell division'; Wikipedia: chicken-embryo red blood cells 'in various stages of division'), 'largely unnoticed' (Embryo Project), and Virchow only 'made the idea famous' in 1855 (Embryo Project, Grokipedia), which stays true though Raspail wrote the motto first; OpenStax says he 'neglected to credit Remak', and the plagiarism charge is put in Weindling's mouth as Wikipedia does. Card no longer says he 'got the credit'. Lures live and wrong: Schleiden and Schwann thought cells form like crystals; Pasteur (life from life, flasks of 1862) is a tempting confusion. Exactly one answer; standard 6th-grade trio; voice clean.

21c410c1d7.why: Lane ruling: science, not math. The question never asks for the product (400 appears only in the card); it asks how the two lens marks combine, which is the optics rule OpenStax states ('the total magnification is the product of the ocular magnification times the objective magnification') and a standard 6th-grade microscope skill. No arithmetic is done to answer it; knowing what the 10x and 40x marks mean together is the whole test. Old tell fixed: 'through both lenses together' is cut and the lenses are given only by their marks, so 'the objective's number alone' (the lens she has just used) and 'the eyepiece's number alone' are live slips beside adding (M2). Exactly one defensible answer; choices in two parallel pairs; card gives the why (the eyepiece enlarges the objective's image, F38). Voice clean.
